𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗔𝗜 𝘁𝗼𝗼𝗹 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝘂𝘀𝗲 𝗺𝗼𝘀𝘁 𝗺𝗶𝗴𝗵𝘁 𝗯𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗿𝗲𝗮𝘀𝗼𝗻 𝘆𝗼𝘂'𝗿𝗲 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘀𝗹𝗼𝘄𝗲𝗿 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝗻 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝗻𝗲𝗲𝗱 𝘁𝗼.

Most people don't choose AI tools.

𝗧𝗵𝗲𝘆 𝗷𝘂𝘀𝘁 𝘂𝘀𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗼𝗻𝗲 𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘆𝗼𝗻𝗲 𝗲𝗹𝘀𝗲 𝗶𝘀 𝘂𝘀𝗶𝗻𝗴.

ChatGPT for everything.
Cursor for every coding task.
Perplexity for every search.
Midjourney for every image.

It feels productive.

But using one tool for every problem is like hiring one person to write, research, design, code, teach and present.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗯𝗲𝘀𝘁 𝗔𝗜 𝘁𝗼𝗼𝗹 𝗱𝗲𝗽𝗲𝗻𝗱𝘀 𝗼𝗻 𝘄𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝘆𝗼𝘂'𝗿𝗲 𝘁𝗿𝘆𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘁𝗼 𝗮𝗰𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗶𝘀𝗵.

For writing, Claude can be a better fit when you need natural tone and long-form structure.

For research, Perplexity is great for web discovery, while NotebookLM shines when you want answers grounded in your own sources.

For images, Midjourney is known for visual quality, while ChatGPT Images makes conversational editing and iteration much easier.

For video, Runway and Veo approach generation differently.

For coding, Cursor and Claude Code offer very different workflows — especially when you move from autocomplete to reasoning across an entire codebase.

For presentations, Canva AI and Gamma solve different parts of the creation process.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗺𝗶𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗸𝗲 𝗶𝘀𝗻'𝘁 𝘂𝘀𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘁𝗵𝗲 “𝘄𝗿𝗼𝗻𝗴” 𝗔𝗜.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗺𝗶𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗸𝗲 𝗶𝘀 𝗮𝘀𝘀𝘂𝗺𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗼𝗻𝗲 𝗔𝗜 𝘁𝗼𝗼𝗹 𝗰𝗮𝗻 𝗯𝗲𝘀𝘁 𝗮𝘁 𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘆𝘁𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗴.

The people getting the most value from AI aren't necessarily using the most tools.

They're using the 𝘳𝘪𝘨𝘩𝘵 tools for the right jobs.

So instead of asking:

“𝗪𝗵𝗶𝗰𝗵 𝗔𝗜 𝘁𝗼𝗼𝗹 𝗶𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗯𝗲𝘀𝘁?”

Ask:

“𝗪𝗵𝗶𝗰𝗵 𝗔𝗜 𝘁𝗼𝗼𝗹 𝗶𝘀 𝗯𝗲𝘀𝘁 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝗷𝗼𝗯?”

𝗧𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗼𝗻𝗲 𝗰𝗵𝗮𝗻𝗴𝗲 𝗰𝗮𝗻 𝗺𝗮𝗸𝗲 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗔𝗜 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸𝗳𝗹𝗼𝘄 𝗺𝘂𝗰𝗵 𝗺𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝗽𝗼𝘄𝗲𝗿𝗳𝘂𝗹.

📌 𝗦𝗮𝘃𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝘀 before choosing your next AI tool.

Sr. Engineer at Nielsen | Ex-Amazon, CARS24 | DTU’17

3h •

There are phases in life where everything hits you at once.

You lose the job.
Your confidence takes a hit.

Home stops feeling peaceful because everyone is worried, frustrated, or asking what happens next.

And suddenly the thing you thought was only a career problem becomes a much bigger crisis.

I have gone through a layoff myself.

And I genuinely believe that if I did not have family, mentors, and a few people who stood by me at the right time, I could have stumbled.

You see, a lot of people attach their identity to work without even realizing it.

You are the engineer.
You are the person earning well.
You are the one who is "doing fine."

Then one announcement comes and suddenly you are unemployed.

If the people around you also start making you feel small at that exact moment, it can completely break someone.

Most people in that situation are not looking for a motivational speech. They already know the worst thing happened.

They need someone who can sit with them without making them feel ashamed.

Someone who says:
→ "Take a few days. We'll figure it out."
→ "Your job is gone. Your ability is not."
→ "Let's fix the resume when you're ready."
→ "I know someone hiring. I'll make the intro."
→ "You do not have to explain yourself to me."

That kind of support matters more than people realize.

Because scars from bad phases stay.
You remember who mocked you when you were down.

But you also remember, for life, who stood beside you when there was nothing to gain from helping you.

And sometimes that person just needs one small push in the right direction.

One referral.
One honest conversation.
A few days of emotional support.

One person who still believes in them when they have stopped believing in themselves.

You never know where someone can go after that.

Maybe they rebuild.
Maybe they land somewhere better.
Maybe years later, they are doing incredibly well.

And you get to know that when they were at their lowest, you helped them stand up again.

That is one of the best things you can do for another person. I absolutely respect Jeet Umat here, he took the time to help out his junior and stood by him.

    StartupFox

    13h •

    Rapido has been fined ₹10 lakh by the Central Consumer Protection Authority for something most riders may never have consciously thought of as manipulation.

    The app would first show a fare. After the rider booked, it could display messages such as “Captains aren’t accepting at ₹60. Try adding +10, +20, +30” or suggest that a higher price meant a higher chance of getting a ride.

    That is the dark pattern in simple words:

    You are not directly forced to pay more. The interface makes you nervous that you may not get the service unless you do.

    CCPA found another layer too. Rapido’s “Set your price” slider showed higher-price choices with positive green messaging, while lowering the amount triggered red or orange warnings. The regulator classified these practices as “confirm shaming” and “interface interference.”

    Rapido argued that the additional payment was voluntary and that its matching system continued searching regardless of whether the rider paid extra.

    But CCPA raised the most important question: if paying more really improves your chances of getting a ride, where is the evidence? The regulator said Rapido did not provide data demonstrating that relationship.

    That is why Nalini U.’s concern about the ₹10 lakh penalty is worth thinking about.

    The difficult question is not only how large the fine should be. It is how much additional money consumers may have paid because the interface made them believe ₹10, ₹20 or ₹30 could materially improve their chances.

    Those tiny amounts barely register individually.

    Multiply them across a large digital platform and behavioural design becomes economics.

    There is a broader lesson here for consumer internet companies. Product design is not neutral. Colours, warnings, countdowns, defaults and button placement can change behaviour just as effectively as a salesperson.

    Good design helps users make a decision.

    A dark pattern makes the platform’s preferred decision feel like the user’s own.

    And as digital businesses increasingly optimise every click, regulators will have to ask not only whether a customer technically consented—but how that consent was engineered.

    Top 25 AWS Services
    (explained in 2 mins or less):

    COMPUTE:

    1 EC2
    ↳ Cloud virtual servers to run apps with full control over operating system.

    2 Lambda
    ↳ Serverless compute that runs code in response to events without managing servers.

    3 ECS
    ↳ Managed container orchestration service for running Docker containers.

    4 EKS
    ↳ Managed Kubernetes service that runs & scales containerized apps.

    5 Auto Scaling
    ↳ Automatically adjusts compute capacity based on demand.

    ===

    STORAGE:

    6 S3
    ↳ Durable object storage for files, backups, media & static content.

    7 EBS
    ↳ Persistent block storage volumes attached to EC2 instances.

    8 EFS
    ↳ Fully managed shared file system accessible by different EC2 instances.

    9 FSx
    ↳ Managed high-performance file systems - Windows File Server.

    10 Snowball
    ↳ Using physical device to transfer large amounts of data into/out of AWS.

    ===

    NETWORKING:

    11 VPC
    ↳ Logically isolated virtual network where you define IP ranges, subnets & routing.

    12 Route 53
    ↳ Scalable DNS service that routes users to apps.

    13 ELB
    ↳ Distributes incoming traffic across different servers for high availability.

    14 CloudFront
    ↳ Global CDN that caches content at edge locations.

    15 Direct Connect
    ↳ Dedicated private network connection from on-premises to AWS.

    ===

    DATABASES:

    16 RDS
    ↳ Managed relational database service.

    17 DynamoDB
    ↳ Fully managed NoSQL key-value database with low latency.

    18 Aurora
    ↳ High-performance relational database compatible with MySQL & PostgreSQL.

    19 Redshift
    ↳ Fully managed data warehouse for large-scale analytics.

    20 ElastiCache
    ↳ In-memory caching service (Redis or Memcached) to reduce database load.

    ===

    SECURITY:

    21 IAM
    ↳ Manages users, roles & permissions for AWS resources.

    22 KMS
    ↳ Managed service for creating & controlling encryption keys.

    23 Cognito
    ↳ User authentication & identity service for web and mobile apps.

    24 GuardDuty
    ↳ Threat detection service that monitors AWS accounts & workloads.

    25 WAF
    ↳ Web application firewall that filters harmful web traffic.
